title: Y-Tz-R
hookLine: yetzer, the impulse, and yatzar, to form, like a potter

cards: A lump of clay sits on a wheel. The potter's hands close around it, wet, the wheel spins, and a wall begins to rise. Push too hard and it collapses.
Too gently and nothing happens. Hebrew has a verb for exactly this, yatzar, to form, and a potter is a yotzer, a former.
From the same root comes a word Jewish tradition uses for something inside a person: yetzer, the impulse, the urge. Yud, tzadi, resh: Y-Tz-R. Clay on the outside, and clay on the inside.

teach.b: Turn this root four ways. First, the dust. In the second chapter of Genesis the verb changes: "Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life."
Formed is yatzar: a potter at work, dust shaped by hand.
Second, the two yuds. In Hebrew, formed, vayyitzer, is spelled with two yuds where one would do.
The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, notices, and reads them as two impulses: the yetzer tov, the good impulse, and the yetzer hara, the bad one. A person is formed with both.
Third, the impulse, which you first met on day one hundred sixty-four. After the flood, the text says plainly, "the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." Imagination is yetzer.
Yet the rabbis refuse to call it simply evil. A midrash on creation says the urge is part of what God called very good, because without it nobody would build a house, marry, or raise a family.

teach.h: THE IMPULSE: RAW MATERIAL, NOT THE ENEMY.
teach.b: For these rabbis, the impulse is raw material, not the enemy.
Fourth, the wheel, from day eight hundred two. Jeremiah goes down to the potter's house.
A vessel goes wrong in the potter's hand, and he doesn't throw out the clay. He makes it again, into another vessel. Then the word comes: "as the clay in the potter's hand, so are ye in My hand."
Formed, and able to be formed again.

how: Jewish teaching speaks of the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara, the good and bad impulses, and Jewish ethical and Hasidic writings treat the work of a life as shaping and channeling the yetzer rather than destroying it.

o: a root for forming, like a potter, and for the impulse
a root for going out, as from Egypt into freedom
a root for narrow straits, a time of real trouble

s: the rabbis treat the bad impulse as pure evil, to be destroyed
a midrash says without it, nobody would build a house, marry or raise a family.
in Genesis 2, man is formed from the dust of the ground
"the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground."

games.q: you're the potter in Jeremiah. the vessel goes wrong in your hands. what do you do?
o: make it again, into another vessel.
games.why: the potter remakes it, and Jeremiah hears: "as the clay in the potter's hand, so are ye in My hand."

practice: Notice an urge that's around today, to check your phone, to snap at someone, to eat something, to quit, and hold it the way a potter holds clay, as material, without fighting it or obeying it yet.
Ask what shape it could take: the urge to snap could become one honest sentence later, the urge to quit a real break. Let your hands rest open, as if something soft were in them.

wordCard.voice: Y-Tz-R. Yud, tzadi, resh: the root of yatzar, to form, like a potter, and of yetzer, the impulse a person is formed with. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: impulse, inclination; from the root of yatzar, to form.

carryVoice: Your line: form. Two yuds, two impulses, one person. Back tomorrow, same hill.
